note: The traveler-facing language catalog — the 50 languages a traveler is most likely to meet, used to populate the world map and the trip language-recommendation score. `nativeAccess` (0-1) estimates how far English alone gets a tourist there; `distance` (1 close … 5 far) is a coarse linguistic distance from English; both are indicative planning estimates, not survey data. `lat`/`lng` place the language's marker on an equirectangular map. status 'available' = a real course exists; 'planned' = placeholder. Courses are NOT built for planned languages yet — these are catalog + map placeholders.

languages.name: Spanish
languages.intro: The highest-leverage language on the list: 20+ countries, close to English, and famously beginner-friendly — regular verbs and phonetic spelling mean a month gets you genuinely functional.

languages.name: Moroccan Darija
languages.intro: Morocco's street Arabic — very different from the Arabic on signs. No verb 'to be' in the present is a gift; five throat sounds and a chat-alphabet that uses numbers (3, 7, 9) are the price of entry. French is a common fallback.

languages.name: French
languages.intro: Reaches far beyond France — much of West and North Africa too. Spelling hides silent letters and nasal vowels, but thousands of words are near-identical to English.

languages.name: Mandarin Chinese
languages.intro: Four tones change meaning, and the writing is non-phonetic — but the grammar is strikingly simple: no tenses, plurals, or conjugation. Pinyin lets you speak without reading characters.

languages.name: Arabic (Modern Standard)
languages.intro: The formal, written pan-Arab language — understood everywhere but spoken natively nowhere; each country has its own dialect. Read right-to-left, with sounds English lacks.

languages.name: Portuguese
languages.intro: Brazil holds most of its speakers. Close to Spanish and to English in vocabulary, but the nasal vowels and swallowed syllables make it sound very different from how it's spelled.

languages.name: Russian
languages.intro: A new alphabet (Cyrillic) you can learn in a weekend, then a case system that reshapes word endings. Like Darija, there's no present-tense 'to be'.

languages.name: German
languages.intro: English's close cousin — huge shared vocabulary — but with cases, gendered nouns, and the verb often flung to the end. English is widely spoken, so this is a 'nice to have'.

languages.name: Japanese
languages.intro: Three scripts and layered politeness levels, but no tones and very regular verbs. Learning the two kana syllabaries first unlocks pronunciation and a lot of signage.

languages.name: Italian
languages.intro: Phonetic, musical, and forgiving — what you see is what you say. Close to Spanish and rich in English cognates; gestures do real grammatical work.

languages.name: Hindi
languages.intro: Lingua franca of northern India, distantly related to English. Word order is subject-object-verb, and English loanwords are everywhere in speech even if the script is new.

languages.name: Turkish
languages.intro: Written in a Latin alphabet that's perfectly phonetic, and gloriously regular — but it builds meaning by stacking suffixes onto words, which takes rewiring.

languages.name: Thai
languages.intro: Five tones and a script with no spaces between words. But the grammar is minimal — no tenses or plurals — so spoken survival Thai comes faster than the writing suggests.

languages.name: Vietnamese
languages.intro: Six tones, but written in a Latin alphabet (with lots of diacritics) thanks to history — so reading is approachable. Words don't change form; grammar is by word order.

languages.name: Greek
languages.intro: Its own alphabet (half of which you already know from math), and a case system. You already speak hundreds of Greek roots — 'telephone', 'democracy', 'analysis'.

languages.name: Korean
languages.intro: Hangul is the rare alphabet you can genuinely learn in a day — it was designed to be easy. No tones. Politeness levels and verb-final order are the real work.

languages.name: Dutch
languages.intro: Sits right between English and German — often intelligible on the page. The Netherlands has among the best English in the world, so this is pure enrichment.

languages.name: Polish
languages.intro: Latin script but famously consonant-dense spelling, plus seven cases. Rewarding and warmly received — few tourists try, and locals notice.

languages.name: Indonesian
languages.intro: Widely called one of the easiest languages for English speakers: Latin script, phonetic, no tones, no verb conjugation, no genders. Plurals are made by saying the word twice.

languages.name: Swahili
languages.intro: East Africa's lingua franca — Latin script, phonetic, and pronounced just as written. Noun-class prefixes are the twist, but pronunciation is easy for English speakers.

languages.name: Hebrew
languages.intro: Read right-to-left, usually without written vowels. Compact and logical once the alphabet clicks; English is common in Israeli tourist areas.

languages.name: Czech
languages.intro: Latin script with accent marks, and a full case system. A few survival phrases go a long way in Prague, where a polite 'dobrý den' is always welcome.

languages.name: Hungarian
languages.intro: Unrelated to its neighbors — an outlier with 18 cases and suffix-stacking. Phonetic once you learn the letters, but genuinely alien grammar; aim for set phrases.

languages.name: Croatian
languages.intro: Latin script, phonetic, and mutually intelligible with Serbian and Bosnian — one effort covers the region. Cases are the main hurdle; the coast is very tourist-friendly.

languages.name: Swedish
languages.intro: Close to English with a lilting pitch accent, and largely intelligible with Norwegian and Danish. English is near-universal, so this is for the joy of it.

languages.name: Norwegian
languages.intro: Often called the easiest Nordic language for English speakers — simple verbs and familiar words. Understanding Swedish and Danish comes largely for free.

languages.name: Danish
languages.intro: Easy on paper, tricky to the ear — Danes swallow sounds, so listening is the challenge. English is spoken almost everywhere.

languages.name: Romanian
languages.intro: A Romance language marooned in a Slavic neighborhood — if you know any Spanish or Italian you'll recognize a lot, with a few surprising Slavic borrowings.

languages.name: Bulgarian
languages.intro: The birthplace of the Cyrillic alphabet. Unusually for a Slavic language, it dropped noun cases — making it one of the easier ones once you read the script.

languages.name: Ukrainian
languages.intro: Cyrillic (slightly different from Russian) and a full case system. A little effort is deeply appreciated; melodic and rich in soft consonants.

languages.name: Persian (Farsi)
languages.intro: Indo-European (a distant English relative) written in Arabic script. Grammar is surprisingly simple — no genders, easy verbs — and the poetry-loving culture rewards effort.

languages.name: Bengali
languages.intro: One of the world's most-spoken languages, across Bangladesh and eastern India. Its own graceful script; subject-object-verb order and no grammatical gender.

languages.name: Tamil
languages.intro: One of the oldest living languages, in southern India and Sri Lanka. Its own script and a formal/spoken split; unrelated to the northern Indian languages.

languages.name: Tagalog (Filipino)
languages.intro: Latin script, loaded with Spanish and English loanwords, and the Philippines has excellent English. Verb-focus markers are the quirk; a warm reception for any attempt.

languages.name: Malay
languages.intro: Very close to Indonesian and equally beginner-friendly: Latin script, phonetic, no tones or conjugation. Reduplication makes plurals ('buku-buku' = books).

languages.name: Khmer
languages.intro: Cambodia's language — and unusually for the region, no tones. The script (the world's longest alphabet) is ornate; spoken survival phrases are the practical goal.

languages.name: Lao
languages.intro: Closely related to Thai and largely mutually intelligible with it. Tonal, with a rounded script; a gentle, unhurried culture that appreciates a few local words.

languages.name: Burmese
languages.native: မြန်မာဘာသာ
languages.intro: Tonal, with a distinctive circular script. English is limited outside tourist hubs, so even a little Burmese goes a long way in Myanmar.

languages.name: Nepali
languages.intro: Shares the Devanagari script and much vocabulary with Hindi. Trekking regions have decent English, but villages don't — 'namaste' and numbers earn real warmth.

languages.name: Sinhala
languages.intro: Sri Lanka's majority language, with a beautifully rounded script. A spoken/written split; even a couple of phrases delight, as few visitors try.

languages.name: Amharic
languages.intro: Ethiopia's language, in the ancient Ge'ez script (a syllabary, not an alphabet). Semitic like Arabic and Hebrew; little English outside Addis, so basics matter.

languages.name: Afrikaans
languages.intro: A daughter of Dutch and the most accessible language for English speakers on the continent — stripped-down grammar, no conjugation. South Africa is English-friendly.

languages.name: Icelandic
languages.intro: A preserved Old Norse — Germanic but with archaic grammar and tongue-twisting place names. Iceland's English is excellent, so this is for love of the language.

languages.name: Georgian
languages.intro: Its own singular alphabet and language family — related to nothing else major. Famous consonant clusters; a fiercely hospitable culture where effort is treasured.

languages.name: Armenian
languages.intro: A lone branch of Indo-European with its own 1,600-year-old alphabet. Distantly related to English; deeply appreciated by a diaspora-proud nation.

languages.name: Mongolian
languages.intro: Now mostly written in Cyrillic, so the script is learnable fast. Vowel harmony and suffix-stacking follow; outside Ulaanbaatar, English is rare.

languages.name: Quechua
languages.intro: The living language of the Andes and the old Inca world, still spoken by millions. Latin script and phonetic; a handful of words transforms how highland communities receive you.

languages.name: Catalan
languages.intro: Not a dialect of Spanish but its own Romance language, spoken in Barcelona, Valencia and the Balearics. Everyone there also speaks Spanish, but Catalan is a point of pride.

languages.name: Zulu
languages.intro: South Africa's most-spoken home language, with distinctive click consonants. Latin script; English is widespread, but a Zulu greeting opens doors warmly.
